sections.overview: Aepus marinus is a tiny ground beetle of north-western European rocky shores. It specializes in the intertidal zone, sheltering in dark, damp crevices and beneath stones near the upper shore. Its pale, flattened body and reduced eyes suit this hidden life between tides.
sections.identification: The adult is reddish yellow to pale and depigmented, flat and nearly parallel-sided, with rudimentary eyes and fine body hairs. It is about 2.3 mm long; reliable body-width, height and mass figures, and sex-specific size measurements, were not found in the sources consulted. It may be confused with the related shore beetle Aepus robinii; compare eye prominence, shoulders and the outline of the wing cases using a specialist key, because published descriptions do not use identical terms for the elytral tip.
sections.habitat: It lives on rocky sea coasts, especially in sheltered crevices, overhangs and beneath stones embedded in coarse sand or gravel. Records place it from the upper part of the middle shore toward the high-water mark, where suitable stones remain damp but provide air-filled refuge as the tide rises. It is recorded around Britain and Ireland and from Brittany north toward southern Norway, although many sites are local.
sections.diet: The beetle is predatory and feeds on tiny arthropods found among shore stones. The Northern Ireland species account specifically reports maritime springtails as prey. No broader prey inventory or measured diet proportions were found, so it is safer to describe it as a small invertebrate predator than to assign it a detailed menu.
sections.behavior: When the tide covers its shore habitat, it retreats into air-filled cracks and spaces beneath stones; it emerges to forage as the water recedes. This tide-linked sheltering lets it occupy ground that is periodically submerged. The available accounts describe a cryptic beetle searched for beneath stones rather than one commonly seen moving in the open.
sections.reproduction: A French coastal invertebrate survey reports a breeding period from April through September. The sources reviewed do not give a well-supported species-specific account of egg laying, larval development or the number of generations, so those details remain open rather than being inferred from other ground beetles.
sections.ecology: Aepus marinus is a specialized predator in the upper intertidal community. Its distribution follows sheltered rocky shores with suitable crevices and stones, while its small prey include maritime springtails. It can occur alongside Aepus robinii, but the two species tend to occupy different shore levels or microhabitats and are not consistently found together at the same sites.
sections.conservation: The sources consulted do not establish a current global IUCN assessment or a measured population trend. Regional accounts describe a restricted, patchy coastal distribution and some local rarity, but these observations alone do not show a species-wide decline. Protecting sheltered rocky shore microhabitats is relevant wherever known colonies occur.
